Maximum entropy methods

Physics × Machine Learning — the least-biased inference

Maximum entropy methods
Saying exactly what the data say — and no more

Faced with incomplete information, which distribution should you assume? Jaynes’ answer: the one with the most entropy consistent with what you know. It is the least-biased choice — maximally noncommittal about everything the data do not pin down. From this single principle flow the Boltzmann distribution, the exponential family, radio-telescope image reconstruction, spectral super-resolution, and much of modern machine learning.

The principle

Among all distributions matching your constraints (a mean, a variance, measured data), choose the one that maximises the Shannon entropy. Any other choice smuggles in information you do not have.

What it delivers

A universal recipe — the Gibbs / exponential-family form — that reproduces statistical mechanics, builds least-biased priors, and regularises hard inverse problems like deconvolution.

What’s inside

The derivation; the standard distributions; the dice problem; the link to statistical mechanics; MaxEnt as inference; image and spectral reconstruction; ML; and generalisations — with five live widgets you can drive (dice, constraints→shape, the canonical ensemble, Burg super-resolution, and a MEM deconvolution).

Where it’s used

Radio interferometry and the Event Horizon Telescope, CMB component separation, weak-lensing mass maps, protein and neural coupling models, and logistic regression — all one idea.

The Contents menu, or Prev / Next (or ← → arrow keys), move through the pages. Several pages carry interactive widgets — drag the sliders and hit the sweep / play buttons. Companion decks cover Bayesian evidence, anomaly detection, and hierarchical models.

From a principle to a formula

Information is quantified by the Shannon entropy — the average surprise of a distribution:

S[p] = − ∑i pi log pi maximal for the uniform distribution (total ignorance), zero for a certainty

Now maximise S subject to what you know: normalisation, and the expectation values of some functions fk (a mean, a variance, a measured correlation). Introduce Lagrange multipliers λk and solve — the stationary point has a universal form:

pi = (1/Z)   exp( −∑k λk fk(xi) ),    Z = ∑i exp( −∑k λk fk ) the Gibbs distribution / exponential family; Z is the partition function that normalises it

The multipliers λk are fixed by making the constraints hold, a job done automatically by the partition function:

− ∂ log Z / ∂λk = ⟨ fk ⟩ = Fk,     Smax = log Z + ∑k λk Fk differentiate log Z to recover the constraints; the maximal entropy is log Z plus the constraint terms
One line, everything downstream. Every named distribution below, all of equilibrium statistical mechanics, and the exponential-family models of machine learning are this formula with different constraint functions fk.

The same rule generates the familiar distributions

Plug different constraints into p ∝ exp(−∑λkfk) and the classic distributions fall out — each is simply the least-biased distribution given that much information.

Bounded support → uniform; a fixed mean on the half-line → exponential; fixed mean and variance → Gaussian; a fixed mean on the non-negative integers → geometric.

Why the Gaussian is everywhere

If all you fix is a mean and a variance, maximum entropy gives the Gaussian. That’s a deep reason the normal distribution is the default: it assumes the least beyond its first two moments.

Constraints = physics

Fix the average energy and you get the Boltzmann distribution; fix average energy and particle number and you get the grand-canonical ensemble. The constraint is the physical knowledge.

Add constraints one at a time — watch the shape appear

Start from total ignorance on a bounded interval (flat). Fix a mean and the least-biased shape becomes an exponential (solved live for λ). Also fix the variance and it becomes a Gaussian — each new fact bends the curve, and nothing else does.

Read-off. Choosing a likelihood or a prior is choosing which moments you claim to know. MaxEnt makes that choice honest: it adds nothing the constraints did not force.

Jaynes’ dice: the principle in miniature

A die is rolled many times; you are told only the average is 4.5, not the fair 3.5. What probabilities should you assign to each face? Maximum entropy gives a unique, honest answer: pi ∝ exp(−λi), with λ tuned so the mean comes out at 4.5.

Left: the least-biased face probabilities for several constrained means — a fair die (λ=0, uniform) tilts smoothly as the mean is raised. Right: the multiplier λ that enforces each mean.

Solve it live — drag the constrained mean

The bars are the least-biased face probabilities pi ∝ e−λi; the multiplier λ is solved (by bisection) so the mean lands exactly where you set it. Nothing else is assumed.

Notice what the answer does not do: it does not invent a story about loaded dice or worn edges. It reproduces exactly the one fact given (the mean) and stays as flat as possible about everything else. A fair die (mean 3.5) recovers the uniform distribution and λ=0.

The entropy concentration theorem

There is a striking justification. Of all the ways to roll the die that are consistent with the constraint, the overwhelming majority produce frequencies close to the maximum-entropy distribution. MaxEnt is not just least-biased — it is what you will almost surely see.

The lesson. Maximum entropy is the unique assignment that is maximally honest about ignorance while exactly respecting the evidence — and it is overwhelmingly the most probable outcome.

Statistical mechanics is maximum entropy

Jaynes’ deepest point (1957): equilibrium statistical mechanics is not a special physical postulate but an inference. Take the constraint to be the average energy ⟨E⟩. Maximum entropy immediately gives the Boltzmann distribution, with the Lagrange multiplier for energy identified as inverse temperature:

pi = (1/Z) e−βEi,    β = 1/kT,    Z = ∑i e−βEi the canonical ensemble — temperature is the multiplier that enforces the energy constraint

Everything in thermodynamics is then a statement about the partition function. The free energy, the entropy and the internal energy are all read off Z:

F = −kT log Z,    S = −∂F/∂T,    ⟨E⟩ = −∂ log Z / ∂β the whole thermodynamic apparatus, from one maximisation

Ensembles = constraints

Microcanonical (fixed E), canonical (fixed ⟨E⟩), grand-canonical (fixed ⟨E⟩, ⟨N⟩) — each ensemble is maximum entropy under a different set of constraints. Nothing else changes.

Why entropy increases

The second law becomes epistemic: as a system evolves toward the constraints you can actually track, the least-biased description is the one of ever-higher entropy.

The canonical ensemble, live — turn the temperature

Equally-spaced energy levels Ei = i (a harmonic ladder). The bars are the Boltzmann populations pi ∝ e−βEi; the panel tracks Z, the average energy ⟨E⟩ and the entropy S as you change T. Cold → everyone in the ground state (S→0); hot → uniform (S maximal).

Unification. The Gibbs distribution of physics and the exponential family of statistics are the same object — maximum entropy under moment constraints. Thermodynamics is inference.

Least-biased priors, and updating with entropy

Maximum entropy is a tool for assigning priors: given only symmetry or moment information, it returns the prior that assumes the least. This grounds many ‘objective’ priors — a uniform prior from bounded support, a Gaussian from a variance, and (via transformation-group arguments) scale-invariant priors like Jeffreys’.

Relative entropy: the general update

When you already have a prior q and learn new constraints, generalise from entropy to relative entropy (minus the KL divergence). Maximise it subject to the constraints to get the updated distribution p closest to q that respects the new information:

maximise   − ∑i pi log( pi / qi )  =  −DKL(p ‖ q)   subject to constraints the minimum-cross-entropy / entropic-updating rule; q is the prior, p the posterior

This entropic inference (Shore & Johnson’s axioms; Caticha) contains Bayes’ theorem as the special case where the constraint is the observed data — updating on data is one kind of entropic update. It is the same ‘change your mind as little as the evidence forces’ discipline, made quantitative.

Two faces, one method. Forward, MaxEnt builds the least-biased model from constraints. Backward, relative-entropy updating revises a prior with new information — and reduces to Bayesian inference when that information is data.

The flagship application: reconstructing an image

Radio interferometers, and the Event Horizon Telescope, do not measure an image — they measure a sparse, noisy sample of its Fourier transform. Inverting that directly gives a ‘dirty’ image riddled with artefacts and negative values. The problem is under-determined: infinitely many images fit the data. Which to choose? The maximum-entropy one — the smoothest, most positive image consistent with the measurements.

maximise   S[image]   subject to   χ2(data) ≈ Ndata the least-structured positive image whose model visibilities fit the data — entropy as the regulariser

A true sky (left), the naive ‘dirty’ image from 26% Fourier coverage (middle, artefact-ridden and partly negative), and the maximum-entropy reconstruction (right, positive and cleaned).

The entropy term does two jobs at once: it enforces positivity (a real sky cannot be negative) and it refuses to invent structure the data do not require. This is the classic Gull–Daniell / Skilling–Bryan maximum-entropy method (MEM) — and a maximum-entropy regulariser is one of the tools behind the first black-hole images.

A live MEM deconvolution — slide the entropy weight

A 1-D toy: two true sources (red) are blurred by a beam and corrupted by noise to give the data (grey). The blue curve is a genuine maximum-entropy reconstruction — it maximises αS[f] − ½χ2 with f = eu forced positive, re-solved as you move α. Too much entropy over-smooths; too little chases the noise.

Regularisation with a reason. Where least-squares over-fits noise and CLEAN assumes point sources, MEM picks the image that adds the least information beyond the data — a principled answer to an ill-posed problem.

Maximum-entropy spectral analysis

Estimating a power spectrum from a short time series is another ill-posed inversion. The periodogram implicitly assumes the data are zero outside the window — a strong, false assumption that smears close peaks together and scatters power into sidelobes. Maximum entropy instead extrapolates the autocorrelation as non-committally as possible, which yields the autoregressive (Burg) spectrum:

P(f) = σ2 / | 1 + ∑k ak e−2πi k f |2 the MaxEnt spectrum is all-pole (autoregressive); the ak come from Burg’s recursion

Two close tones in a 40-sample noisy record. The periodogram (grey) blurs them into one leakage-filled lobe; the maximum-entropy estimate (blue) resolves both at their true frequencies.

By not assuming the signal vanishes outside the record, MaxEnt achieves super-resolution — separating features finer than the naive 1/N frequency limit. It is a workhorse in geophysics, radar, and the analysis of short or gappy astronomical time series.

Push two tones together — and watch which method keeps them apart

Two sinusoids in a short, noisy 48-sample record. The grey curve is the periodogram (FFT power); the blue curve is the maximum-entropy / Burg autoregressive spectrum, both computed live in your browser. Slide the tones together: the periodogram fuses them into one lobe long before MaxEnt gives up.

The same idea again. Don’t pad with zeros you never measured. Extrapolate with the least added structure — and close peaks emerge that the FFT cannot separate.

Maximum entropy under the hood of ML

Many of the models machine learning reaches for by default — logistic regression, softmax classifiers, exponential-family GLMs, energy-based nets — are maximum-entropy distributions in disguise. Here is the flagship case, worked explicitly.

Explicit example: logistic regression is maximum entropy

We want a classifier p(y|x). Suppose the only thing we insist on is that, on average over the data, the model reproduces a set of feature statistics fk(x,y) — for example each input times the label. Ask for the distribution with the most entropy subject to those expectation constraints. Maximising the conditional entropy with Lagrange multipliers λk gives exactly the softmax form, and for two classes, the logistic function:

p(y | x) = exp( ∑k λk fk(x,y) ) / Z(x)   →2-class   p(y=1|x) = σ( w·x + b ) the Gibbs form again — a softmax over classes; λk become the weights w

And the equations that fix the weights are precisely the maximum-entropy moment-matching conditions: choose w so the model’s expected feature statistics equal the empirical ones.

∑i fk(xi, yi)  =  ∑i ∑y p(y|xi)   fk(xi, y) ‘model feature-averages = data feature-averages’ — identical to maximum-likelihood logistic regression

Left: a MaxEnt classifier fitted by moment-matching (red) lands on the identical decision boundary and weights as a hand-coded maximum-likelihood logistic regression (Newton/IRLS, dashed). Right: at the solution the model’s feature expectations exactly equal the empirical moments — the defining MaxEnt condition.

Both fits are coded from scratch — one maximises entropy by moment-matching, the other maximises the logistic likelihood by Newton’s method — and they agree to three decimals (w = 4.54, 2.96 either way), with the moment-matching bars coinciding exactly. “Find the least-biased distribution matching these feature averages” and “fit a logistic regression” are the same computation. These MaxEnt models were the workhorse of classical NLP (Berger et al. 1996).

The same idea, everywhere else

Exponential families & GLMs

Every exponential-family likelihood is the maximum-entropy distribution for its sufficient statistics. Generalised linear models and graphical models inherit the structure — and the moment-matching fit.

Energy-based & Boltzmann machines

Boltzmann machines and Markov random fields are Gibbs distributions p ∝ e−E(x); training matches model expectations to data expectations — the same MaxEnt condition. Pairwise (Ising/Potts) models too.

Maximum-entropy reinforcement learning

MaxEnt RL adds an entropy bonus to the reward, yielding policies as random as possible while still achieving return — more robust and explorative (soft actor-critic). Maximum-entropy inverse RL infers rewards by the same principle.

Not a coincidence. When a model has the softmax / exponential / energy form, a maximum-entropy principle is behind it — and it explains why that form is the right, least-biased choice given the features you decided to match.

The wider entropy family

Relative entropy & cross-entropy

The KL divergence DKL(p‖q) generalises entropy to a ‘distance’ from a reference q; minimising it under constraints is the general MaxEnt update, and cross-entropy is the loss that trains most classifiers.

Maximum caliber

Apply the principle to whole trajectories rather than states and you get maximum caliber — a MaxEnt route to dynamics and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics (Presse et al. 2013).

Tsallis & Rényi entropies

Non-additive generalisations of Shannon entropy give heavy-tailed (power-law) maximum-entropy distributions, proposed for systems with long-range correlations — useful, though their physical status is debated.

Links to evidence & MDL

Maximum entropy connects to the minimum description length principle and, through the partition function, to the Bayesian evidence — different faces of ‘prefer the simplest adequate description’.

Shore & Johnson: why this functional

Remarkably, the entropy is not an arbitrary choice. Shore & Johnson (1980) showed that a few consistency axioms — that inference should not depend on irrelevant coordinate choices or on how independent subsystems are grouped — single out maximum (relative) entropy as the unique consistent rule for updating a distribution under constraints.

Not just convenient — forced. Under mild consistency requirements, maximum entropy is the only method that avoids introducing correlations or structure the data never justified.

Maximum entropy across astronomy and cosmology

Radio interferometry & the EHT

The classic MEM application: reconstructing sky brightness from sparse (u,v) visibilities. A maximum-entropy regulariser (in eht-imaging’s regularised-maximum-likelihood framework) was among the methods behind the first images of the M87* and Sgr A* black holes.

CMB component separation

Separating the CMB from Galactic foregrounds across frequency maps is an ill-posed unmixing solved with maximum-entropy methods (Hobson et al.) — the least-biased separation consistent with the multi-frequency data.

Weak-lensing mass maps

Reconstructing the projected dark-matter distribution from noisy galaxy shears is under-determined; maximum-entropy reconstruction produces positive, artefact-controlled mass maps (Marshall et al.).

Deconvolution & spectra

Sharpening images blurred by a PSF, and estimating power spectra from short or gappy light curves, are everyday MaxEnt / MEM tasks across optical, X-ray and time-domain astronomy.

Primordial power spectrum

Reconstructing the primordial spectrum P(k) from CMB and large-scale-structure data is a regularised inversion where maximum-entropy and related penalties tame the noise amplification.

Least-biased modelling

Wherever a distribution must be assumed from limited moments — velocity distributions, luminosity functions, priors on nuisance parameters — MaxEnt supplies the honest default.

Beyond astronomy: entropy as an inference engine

Statistical mechanics

The founding application (Jaynes): the canonical and grand-canonical ensembles, and the whole apparatus of thermodynamics, derived as maximum-entropy inference under energy (and number) constraints.

Inferring interaction networks

Pairwise maximum-entropy (Ising/Potts) models fit to correlations infer the couplings in a system. In biophysics, direct coupling analysis predicts protein 3-D contacts from sequence covariation; in neuroscience, MaxEnt models capture collective firing states.

Turbulence & fluids

Maximum-entropy and maximum-caliber arguments predict coherent-structure statistics and closures where first-principles solutions are out of reach.

Plasma & kinetic theory

MaxEnt closures reconstruct velocity distribution functions from a few moments — a practical tool in plasma physics and rarefied-gas dynamics.

Ecology, economics, linguistics

Species-abundance distributions, income distributions and word frequencies are all modelled as maximum-entropy outcomes under the relevant constraints — the principle travels far beyond physics.

Non-equilibrium dynamics

Maximum caliber extends the method to time series and trajectories, giving least-biased models of stochastic dynamics and rate processes.

One engine, many fields. Whenever you must infer a distribution from limited constraints — not just measure one — maximum entropy is the least-biased answer, and the exponential form keeps reappearing for that reason.

Where to be careful

Which constraints?

The output is only as good as the constraints you impose. Choosing which moments or features to fix is a modelling decision, not automatic — and different choices give different ‘least-biased’ answers. The principle disciplines the step after that choice.

Which entropy / base measure?

On continuous spaces the entropy depends on a base measure (the ‘q’ in relative entropy); results are coordinate-dependent unless it is chosen deliberately. Relative entropy, not plain Shannon entropy, is the coordinate-safe object.

The regularisation strength

In image and spectral reconstruction, how hard to weight entropy vs data fit is a real choice. Set it so the misfit χ2 matches the number of data (or by cross-validation / Bayesian evidence) rather than by eye.

Not a licence to ignore priors

MaxEnt is powerful but not a substitute for genuine prior knowledge. Where you truly know structure, encode it — as a base measure or explicit prior — rather than letting flatness erase it.

Honest, not magic. Maximum entropy guarantees you add nothing beyond your stated constraints — it cannot rescue badly chosen constraints or a missing base measure. Used with care, it is the most defensible default there is.

Software for maximum-entropy methods

General MaxEnt & optimisation

maxentropy (Ed Schofield’s MaxEnt models), PyMaxEnt (moment problems), and scipy.optimize for the Lagrange/convex problem. scikit-learn LogisticRegression is a MaxEnt classifier.

Image reconstruction

eht-imaging (EHT; entropy among its regularisers), SMILI, and MEM in radio packages CASA, MIRIAD and difmap. General image MEM in scikit-image deconvolution and legacy MEMSYS.

Spectral analysis

spectrum (Python; Burg & other AR/MaxEnt estimators) and scipy.signal for parametric spectra and periodograms to compare against.

Coupling models (Ising/Potts)

plmc, CCMpred and PlmDCA for direct coupling analysis; coniii and ACE for inverse-Ising / pairwise MaxEnt fitting in biophysics and neuroscience.

Getting started. For a distribution from moments, scipy.optimize on the dual is a few lines. For imaging, start from eht-imaging or your instrument’s MEM task; for spectra, the spectrum package’s Burg estimator; for coupling models, a DCA library.
